A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RobotArena∞. The main text, figures, equations, and complete Appendices A–I are readable and can be matched across versions.

before.justification: v1 reports original policy evaluations, perturbation experiments, human preference judgments, and a real-versus-simulation comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports expanded policy comparisons, revised automated scores, and additional human preference results.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 changes a central evaluation component: v1 scores shuffled images without simulator state, whereas v2 uses ordered frames with privileged object and robot states. The real-to-sim reconstruction pipeline and Bradley–Terry ranking method remain unchanged; the expanded depth-scaling explanation already appeared in v1 Appendix B.2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate BridgeSim, DROIDSim, RH20TSim, the four reproduced SIMPLER environments, and the real/simulated carrot-placement task. Background, color, and object-pose perturbation coverage is retained. Adding policies does not add datasets or task scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds X-VLA and the open-pi-zero reimplementation of π0 to the four existing policies in the benchmark, perturbation, human-preference, and SIMPLER comparisons. The real-world comparison still evaluates only Octo, SpatialVLA, and RoboVLM.

E3.justification: Automated evaluation switches from shuffled visual observations to temporally ordered frames plus simulator state, substantially changing scoring conditions. Averaging the final 30% of frames remains unchanged. The reported human comparison count increases from 7,104 to 8,749, although v2 Appendix I retains 7,104.

E4.justification: The existing background, color, and object-pose robustness analyses gain evidence for two additional policies under the revised scorer. Section 4.1 removes v1's reported few-shot versus zero-shot comparison and comparison of three score-aggregation choices. The real/simulation case study and appendix diagnostic analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report SEM for automated benchmark scores and use the same robust sandwich estimator for Bradley–Terry confidence intervals. Appendix I's statistical procedure is unchanged, with no added seed, repeated-run, or significance-testing protocol.

E6.justification: Benchmark scores are extensively replaced: BridgeSim Octo changes from 51.96% in v1 Figure 6 to 28.00% in v2 Figure 7, under different scoring conditions. New BridgeSim results place open-pi-zero at 45.55% and X-VLA at 42.08%. Human rankings and Figure 9's SIMPLER results also change; Figure 8's real/simulation results remain identical. These are not same-setting performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: The calibration losses, geometric reconstruction equations, controller-identification objective, perturbation definitions, and Bradley–Terry derivations are retained. No mathematical assumptions, proofs, or formal results are added or substantively revised.

C1.justification: The four stated contributions remain automated real-to-sim translation, scalable human/VLM benchmarking, extensive policy evaluation, and generalization findings. The introduction and conclusion update policy and preference counts without changing these contributions or the retained largest-scale evaluation claim.

C2.justification: v2 adds the 'Spatial Paradox' hypothesis about implicit spatial learning from multiview pretraining, expands the overfitting interpretation, and attributes SIMPLER's higher scores to limited and biased scenario selection. It strengthens human/VLM agreement to an exact-ranking claim, although Figures 6–7 reverse the nearly tied Octo/SpatialVLA ordering. The stated wrist-camera and contact-dynamics limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 identifies the evaluator as Gemini 2.5 Pro and specifies X-VLA-0.9B, the open-pi-zero implementation, and single-view fine-tuned policies for the new comparisons. Existing reconstruction, segmentation, controller, perturbation, and annotation details remain in the appendices. The main-text depth-calibration expansion repeats previously available appendix information.

R1.justification: The generalist-policy survey is replaced by focused positioning against automated real-to-sim systems. New discussion contrasts Phone2Proc, Scalable Real2Sim, Re3Sim, and RialTo with the proposed input and supervision requirements. This substantively revises the nearest-work comparison, beyond bibliography deduplication and added policy references.

P1.justification: v2 condenses and rewrites several introductory and methodological passages, absorbs Section 3.1 into Section 3, and introduces a dedicated benchmarking-results subsection. Authorship, affiliations, and acknowledgments also change. The overall seven-section organization and Appendix A–I structure remain.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is redesigned to show state-conditioned scoring and progression examples. Main result plots gain policy series, revised legends, and axis ranges; the human and automated ranking figures exchange numbers. Several figures are repositioned or resized, while the basic display types and all appendix figures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The additional policies and focused real-to-sim comparisons improve relevance and context. However, v2 leaves consequential reporting inconsistencies: Figure 6 reports 8,749 comparisons while Appendix I reports 7,104, and Appendix H still identifies Octo as the RH20TSim leader despite revised results favoring RoboVLM. The exact human/VLM ranking-agreement claim also overstates the plotted evidence. These benefits and reliability problems prevent a confident net quality judgment.
